name: Lukács Thermal Bath
description: A thermal bath in Buda's Felhévíz district whose springs have been used for centuries. Wikipedia traces bathing on the site to at least the 12th century, and the present complex developed from the 1880s onward. Over time it became a favourite of Hungarian writers, composers and filmmakers, and it still has a medical side.

children.text: The Lukács Bath (Szent Lukács gyógyfürdő) lies on the Buda side in the 2nd district, in an area the Middle Ages called Felhévíz, a name that refers to its thermal springs. Wikipedia says thermal baths have been used on the site since at least the 12th century, by the Knights Hospitaller. During the Ottoman period the spring water powered a mill, and a wall inside the bath is described as a remnant of the Ottoman Császár powder mill.

The present bath grew from development that began in the mid-1880s. A Hungarian cultural article says Palotay bought the area from the treasury in 1884 and named it Szent Lukács, Saint Luke, after which the bath became a public limited company in 1893, with a mud bath, spa hotel and public steam bath. Rezső Ray the elder designed the hotel, and Rezső Hikisch unified the facade in a Classicist-Biedermeier style in the 1920s. A drinking-cure hall was built in 1937, during the First International Congress of Bathing.

Lukács was well known across the Monarchy and Europe, and until the Széchenyi and Gellért baths were completed it was Budapest's most significant thermal bath. Budappest, a travel site, names the composer Zoltán Kodály as a regular guest and the writers Gyula Illyés and Tibor Déry and the filmmakers Károly Makk and Péter Bacsó as notable patrons. In the courtyard and walls are gratitude plaques left by visitors who felt healed. Many were lost in the Second World War, and the surviving ones were built into the walls during renovation.

After the war a hospital moved into the former hotel, and the rheumatology institute based there from 1951 has since been reorganised, while Lukács still combines medical treatment with bathing. Wikipedia lists thermal pools of different temperatures, swimming pools, a wellness section, sauna facilities and a gallery. A restoration completed in 2013 is reported to have received an ICOMOS award. Across Frankel Leó út is the Malom Lake area, where a building known as the Turkish bath was never Turkish at all, but a people's steam bath built by Palotay.
Good to know

The bath's official site lists trams 4, 6, 17 and 19, buses 9 and 109 and the HÉV suburban railway (Margit híd stop) as ways to reach it; check BKK's journey planner for the best route to Frankel Leó út 25-29.
Facilities, sauna rules and which pools are available differ by section, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and rules.
Look for the gratitude plaques in the walls and the drinking-cure hall from 1937.

historyIntro: The Lukács Baths sit on springs that have been used for bathing for centuries, and the complex still carries traces of its Ottoman past inside its walls.

children.text: According to the bath's own history, thermal baths have been used on this site since at least the twelfth century, reportedly by the Knights Hospitallers. A wall inside the complex is a remnant of a former Ottoman powder mill, the Császár mill, which used the hot spring water as a source of power. The neighbouring Császár Thermal Bath is described as the oldest continuously operating thermal bath in Budapest: it was originally built by Szokoli Mustafa and redesigned in 1844 by József Hild.

The first spa hotel on the site was completed in the 1880s and named after Saint Luke. A drinking-water hall followed in 1937 and a health clinic in 1979. The water is rich in calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates and contains a substantial amount of fluoride. Part of the complex belongs to the National Institute of Rheumatology and Physiotherapy. Much of this history rests on the bath's own account, so treat individual dates as the operator's, not as independently verified.

name: Rudas Thermal Bath
description: A Buda bath beside Erzsébet Bridge whose Ottoman core, an octagonal pool under a dome on eight columns, dates from the 16th century. Later wings add a swimming pool and a modern wellness area. Its gender-separated apron bathing was added to Hungary's national intangible heritage list in October 2026.

children.text: The Rudas Baths stand at Döbrentei tér 9 on the Buda bank, at the foot of Gellért Hill beside Erzsébet Bridge. Wikipedia describes it as founded in 1571 or 1572 under Ottoman rule, when Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, the governor of Buda, commissioned it. Other sources give a work period of 1566 to 1572 for converting the earlier building, so the exact dates vary by source. A guide from We Love Budapest adds that Hospitaller knights had built a hospital and a bath on the site under King Béla IV.

The Ottoman core is the main thing to see. An octagonal pool lies under a hemispherical dome supported by eight columns, with small windows letting in light. A 2012 article gives the dome a diameter of about ten metres. The Ottoman-period name, Jesil Direkli ilidzsa, is translated as green-columned bath, though We Love Budapest notes that archaeologists have never found the green column, and offers one theory that the later name Rudas comes from a Serbian and Bosnian shortening meaning mineral-water bath.

The complex grew in stages. Xpatloop reports that the swimming pool was built in 1896 and that from 1936 the thermal bath was visited exclusively by men. A 19th-century classicist wing houses an indoor pool, and the Juventus wing, on the site of a former mineral-water bottling plant, opened in 2014 as a modern wellness area with a facade of girih patterns. Wikipedia notes a comprehensive interior renovation that ended with a reopening at the beginning of 2006.

Rudas also carries a social tradition. A Time Out report dated 20 October 2026 says that the gender-separated bathing in cotton aprons was added to the National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage, and that the listing protects the practice, not the building. Visitors should check the official site for which days are single-sex and which are mixed, because those arrangements have changed over time. Wikipedia also records that the opening scene of the 1988 film Red Heat was filmed here.
Good to know
The bath's official site lists trams 19, 41, 56 and 56A and several bus lines as ways to reach Döbrentei tér; check BKK's journey planner for the best route.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the schedule of men's, women's and mixed days, which have changed over time.
The baths stand at the foot of Gellért Hill, so the hill is close by for a walk before or after your visit.

heroImage.alt: The plain white street facade of the Rudas Thermal Bath with its name above the windows

historyIntro: The Rudas Baths are one of the few places in Budapest where you can still bathe in an Ottoman hammam: an octagonal pool under a dome, beside the Danube, that is more than four hundred years old.

historySections.heading: An Ottoman bath on the Danube

children.text: The baths were founded in 1571 or 1572 during Ottoman rule, commissioned by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, who was governor (beylerbey) of Buda from 1566 to 1578. They keep many elements of a hammam, including an Ottoman dome and an octagonal pool, and are described as echoing the monumental Ottoman bath buildings of Istanbul. They stand at Döbrentei tér, on the Buda side of Erzsébet Bridge, at the foot of Gellért Hill.

historySections.heading: Thermal water and a new opening

children.text: The thermal water is slightly radioactive and contains sulphate, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate and a significant amount of fluoride. The complex has six therapy pools and one swimming pool, with temperatures between 10 and 42 degrees Celsius. After a comprehensive interior renovation the baths reopened at the beginning of 2006.

name: Palatinus Bath
description: Budapest's first outdoor beach on Margaret Island, opened in 1919 and expanded in the 1930s with a modernist changing building and a wave pool. Its thermal-well water, historic mosaics and year-round indoor wellness section, added in a 2017 reconstruction, make it one of the city's most layered bathing complexes.

children.text: The Palatinus Strandfürdő is a bathing complex on Margaret Island, fed by the island's thermal wells. According to We Love Budapest it opened on 15 June 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach, and Hungarian Wikipedia places the first opening in the era of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, before the Danube embankment had walls. It closed after a year for construction, and the new bath opened permanently in August 1921 with a large main pool and further cold and warm pools.

The best-known building was added in 1937, when the elder István Janáky and Károly Szőke designed a modernist reception and changing block with terraces and spiral staircases, together with a wave pool. Hungarian Wikipedia lists the architectural style as Bauhaus, and the Budapest Info page for the bath carries the same label in its title. We Love Budapest records that the plan caused public debate and that the architect Virgil Bierbauer defended it in the journal Tér és Forma.

Art and sculpture have always been part of the site. At the entrance stood a sculpture by Géza Csorba and, in the ticket hall, a wall painting by István Pekáry referring to an Ady poem, both damaged or destroyed in the war. The painting was restored in the 2017 reconstruction, and Csorba's work was recarved in the 1960s. The wave pool carries a surrealist mosaic by Endre Bálint, whose style is compared to Miró's. Before the Second World War, the bath's continuous water surface made it Europe's largest outdoor bath, according to We Love Budapest.

The reconstruction of 2016-17, carried out by Archikon, winterised the building and added indoor thermal pools, a sauna section and therapy rooms, so the complex now runs outdoor and indoor sections that are not necessarily available at the same times. A 2025 news report states that the indoor section stays open year-round while the outdoor pools work only in the warm season. The wave machine, a piston-driven one, was renovated in 2026, and only a few such machines remain in Hungary, with Budapest having two, at Palatinus and Gellért.
Good to know
Outdoor pools and slides are seasonal, while the indoor wellness and thermal section is described as available through the year, so check which parts are running on your date.
Look for the mosaic by Endre Bálint at the wave pool and the Pekáry wall painting in the ticket hall.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and house rules before travelling to Margaret Island.

historyIntro: Palatinus opened in 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach and grew into one of the largest open-air baths in Europe. A 1937 expansion, postwar changes and a 2017 reconstruction shaped what visitors see today.

children.text: We Love Budapest records that the bath opened on 15 June 1919 as Budapest's first outdoor beach, with water from the island's thermal wells, which 19th-century drilling by Vilmos Zsigmondy had made possible. Károly Arvé and Márton Nagy designed the first beach, which had no reception building yet. Hungarian Wikipedia says it closed after a year so that construction could begin and that the new bath opened permanently in August 1921, with a large main pool and further cold and warm pools. Before the Second World War its continuous water surface of about five thousand square metres made it the largest outdoor bath in Europe, according to We Love Budapest.

In 1937 the elder István Janáky and Károly Szőke designed the central changing building, a modernist block with terraces and spiral staircases, together with the wave pool. The plan was debated in public, and the architect Virgil Bierbauer defended it in the journal Tér és Forma against critics who wanted the park setting left intact. Wave pools were then still new in Budapest: We Love Budapest notes that the first in the city was at Csillaghegy in 1927 and that Palatinus was the third. The war later destroyed sculpture and a wall painting at the entrance.

After the war the bath was restored. Hungarian Wikipedia lists a ten-thousand-square-metre sunbathing lawn added in 1958, a new restaurant in 1965, an additional area with playgrounds and a football pitch in 1975, and a five-lane slide in the 1980s. A mosaic by Endre Bálint was added at the wave pool in the 1960s. In 2002 the pools received modern filtration, and in 2016-17 the monument-protected reconstruction by Archikon winterised the main building and added a covered section with thermal and wellness facilities, so the bath could work throughout the year. The destroyed Ady-poem wall painting was restored at the same time.

stories.title: A public argument over the 1937 building

children.text: According to the We Love Budapest history of the bath, the 1937 plan for a new reception and changing block caused public debate. Some critics wanted the parkland setting of the island left intact. The architect Virgil Bierbauer defended the new building in the journal Tér és Forma.
